en: This is the Upaniṣad of Nirukta: whatever one pursues, that he becomes. If he pursues dharma, that very thing arises for him. If he pursues knowledge, he becomes immortal. If he pursues desire, he enters this cycle of birth; he joins this womb. Herein, this mind arises from phlegm and semen. From phlegm comes chyle; from chyle, blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; from fat, sinews; from sinews, bones; from bones, marrow; and from marrow, semen.

When this semen is emitted into the womb, a person comes into being. If there is an excess of semen, one becomes male; if there is an excess of blood, one becomes female; if both are equal, one becomes a neuter; and if the semen is divided, one becomes twin-born. Through the union of semen and blood, and through the union of mother and father, how is this body further constrained? Having remained for one night, it becomes *kalala*; after five nights, it becomes a bubble (*budbuda*); after seven nights, it becomes a mass (*peśī*).

After fourteen days, it becomes an *arbuda*. Remaining in the womb for twenty-five nights, it becomes a *ghana*. After one month, it becomes solid (*kaṭhina*). Within two months, the head is formed. In three months, the neck is delineated. In four months, the skin is delineated. In the fifth month, nails and hair are delineated. In the sixth, the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears come into being. In the seventh, it becomes capable of movement. In the eighth, it forms conceptual determinations through the intellect (*buddhi*).

In the ninth [month], he becomes complete in all his limbs. "Dead I was born again, and born I died again. Indeed, thousands of various wombs have been inhabited by me. Various foods were eaten; various breasts were drunk from. Various mothers were seen, as well as fathers and friends. Oppressed and with face turned downward, the creature is thus endowed [with a body]. Therefore, I shall practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga, [seeking] the twenty-fifth principle (puruṣa). Thus [he reflects].
Then, in the tenth month, it is born. Once born, touched by the vital wind (*vāyu*), it does not remember its birth or death, nor its good or evil deeds at the end; such is the measure of this body.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Niruktopaniṣad*.

The head consists of one hundred and eight joints and eight skull-bones (*kapāla*). There are sixteen fatty membranes (*vapāpalāni*). There are nine hundred sinews (*snāyu*). A man has seven hundred vital points (*marman*). There are thirty-five million hairs (*roma*). The heart consists of eight skull-bones. The tongue consists of twelve skull-bones. The testicles are two firm, well-formed wings. Beyond that are the generative organ, the anus, and the womb; this [organism] grows through the sprinkling of food and drink. It is said that they are produced from one another through karma.

Knowledge and action follow him, as does his prior wisdom. Immersed in the great darkness of ignorance and overwhelmed by the pairs of opposites consisting of old age, death, hunger, thirst, sorrow, anger, malice, greed, delusion, pride, fear, envy, jealousy, and arrogance, he is liberated from this state, reaching the end of the process of rapid transformation through straightforwardness.

Thus, having departed from this body like a great meteor in the blink of an eye, surrounded by his own natural elements, and having assumed a fiery body, he experiences the fruit corresponding to his karma; upon the exhaustion of that, he returns again to this world.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Niruktopaniṣad.
